senses: to bring or summon before a tribunal, complain of, accuse
la:verb:arripio.html:
ar-rĭpĭo (adr-, B. and K.; arr-, Lachm., Ritschl, Fleck., Merk., Rib., K. and H., Weissenb., Halm), rĭpŭi, reptum, 3, v. a.
rapio
,
to seize, snatch, lay hold of, draw a person or thing to one's self (esp. with haste).
In gen.
Lit.: ut eum eriperet, manum arripuit mordicus: Vix foras me abripui atque effugi,; cf. the first of the words following, formed by Plaut. after the manner of Aristophanes: Quodsemelarripides Numquampostreddonides, Ritschl: gladium,; : pugionem,: securim,: arma,: cultrum,: telum, vestimenta,: arcus Arripit,: ensem,: saxum,: pileum vel galerum,: scutum e strage,: sagittam et scutum,: clipeum,: aliquem barbā,: manu,: aliquam comā,: caput capillo,: manum alicujus, Auct. B. G. 8, 23; .—
Trop., to take to one's self, procure, appropriate, seize: Arripe opem auxiliumque ad hanc rem,: vox et gestus subito sumi et aliunde adripi non potest,: cognomen sibi ex Aeliorum imaginibus adripuit,: non debes adripere maledictum ex trivio aut ex scurrarum aliquo convicio,: libenter adripere facultatem laedendi,: aliquid ad reprehendendum,: impedimentum pro occasione arripere,—
Transf.
In gen., to seize, lay hold of, take possession of, secure: Sublimem medium arriperem, et capite pronum in terram statuerem,: simul arripit ipsum Pendentem,: medium arripit Servium,: quando arripuerit te spiritus Domini malus,; so : Existit sacer ignis et urit corpore serpens, Quamcumque arripuit partim,: quemcumque patrem familias adripuissetis ex aliquo circulo,you might have taken,: nisi forte eum (dolorem) dicis, qui simul atque adripuit, interficit,: vitulum,: leones,: navem,: arrepto repente equo,: cohortes arreptas in urbem inducit,.—Trop., of the mind, to seize upon with eagerness or haste, to learn quickly or with avidity: pueri celeriter res innumerabiles adripiunt,: quas (sc. Graecas litteras) quidem sic avide adripui, quasi diuturnam sitim explere cupiens,; cf. : Quarum studium etsi senior arripuerat,: quaerit Socrates unde animum adripuerimus, si nullus fuerit in mundo,: quod animus adriperet aut exciperet extrinsecus ex divinitate,.—
As a judicial t. t., to bring or summon before a tribunal, to complain of, accuse (cf. rapio; esp. freq. of those who are complained of after leaving their office): eum te adripuisse, a quo non sis rogatus,: ad quaestionem ipse adreptus est,: tribunus plebis consules abeuntes magistratu arripuit,: arreptus a P. Numitorio Sp. Oppius,: arreptus a viatore,: quaestor ejus in praejudicium aliquot criminibus arreptus est,: inter Sejani conscios arreptus,.—Hence,
In Horace, to attack with ridicule or reproach, to ridicule, satirize: Primores populi arripuit populumque tributim, Sat. 2, 1, 69: luxuriam et Nomentanum arripe mecum,.

la:verb:arrigo.html:
ar-rĭgo (adr-, Dietsch, Halm; arr-, Fleck., Rib., Weissenb.), rexi, rectum, 3, v. a.
rego
,
to set up, raise, erect (not used by Cic., but for it he employs erigere).
Lit.: leo comas arrexit,; so : aurīs,; so ; ; (translatio a pecudibus, Don. ad Ter. l. c.; cf. opp. demittere aures,): linguam,: tollit se arrectum quadrupes,; so ; 2, 206 et saep.—
Trop., to encourage, animate, rouse, excite: eos non paulum oratione suā Marius adrexerat,: cum spes arrectae juvenum,when hope was aroused,: arrectae stimulis haud mollibus irae,: Etruria atque omnes reliquiae belli adrectae,are in commotion, are roused, Gerl.: adrectā omni civitate,excited with wonder,.—Esp. freq. arrigere aliquem or animos, to incite, rouse the mind or courage to something, to direct to something (sometimes with ad aliquam rem): vetus certamen animos adrexit, Kritz: sic animis eorum adrectis,; ; : arrexere animos Itali,: his animum arrecti dictis,: arrecti ad bellandum animi sunt, (cf. erigo).—Hence, arrectus (adr-), a, um, P. a., set upright; hence, steep, precipitous (rare): pleraque Alpium ab Italiā sicut breviora, ita arrectiora sunt,: saxa arrectiora, Sol. c. 14.

la:verb:arrogo.gloss: to claim as one's own, arrogate to oneself, assume
senses: to claim as one's own, arrogate to oneself, assume
to confer upon or procure for someone
to ask or inquire of someone, question
to associate with someone, place by the side of someone
la:verb:arrogo.html:
ar-rŏgo (adr-, Fleck., B. and K., Dietsch, Halm, Weissenb.; arr-, Holder, Dinter; Keller uses both forms), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.
Jurid. and polit. t. t.
To ask or inquire of one, to question: Venus haec volo adroget te, * ; cf. .—*
Alicui, t. t., to add one officer to another, to associate with, place by the side of: cui consuli dictatorem adrogari haud satis decorum visum est patribus,.—
To take a homo sui juris in the place of a child, to adopt (v. arrogatio), ; cf. ; ; —Hence,
Transf.
To appropriate that which does not belong to one, to claim as one's own, to arrogate to one's self, to assume: quamquam mihi non sumo tantum, judices, neque adrogo, ut, etc.,: non enim mihi tantum derogo, tametsi nihil adrogo, ut, etc.,: sapientiam sibi adrogare,: ego tantum tibi tribuo,

quantum mihi fortasse arrogo, : Quod ex alienā virtute sibi adrogant, id mihi ex meā non concedunt,: Nihil adrogabo mihi nobilitatis aut modestiae,: Nec sibi cenarum quivis temere arroget artem,.—

Poet.: alicui aliquid, to adjudge something to another as his own, to confer upon or procure for (opp. abrogare): Scire velim, chartis pretium quotus adroget annus,: decus arrogavit,: nihil non arroget armis,adjudge every thing to arms, think every thing must yield to,.— Hence, arrŏgans (adr-), antis, P. a., acc. to II. A., appropriating something not one's own; hence, assuming, arrogant (syn.: superbus, insolens, ferox).
Lit.: si essent adrogantes, non possem ferre fastidium,: Induciomarus iste minax atque adrogans,; : ne arrogans in praeripiendo populi beneficio videretur,: pigritia adrogantior,: adrogantissima persuasio,.—
As a consequence of assumption, haughty, proud, overbearing, insolent (cf. arrogantia, I. B.): proponit inania mihi nobilitatis, hoc est hominum adrogantium nomina,: de se persuasio,: crudelitas adrogans,: dictum,: consilium,: moderatio,: adversus superiores tristi adulatione, adrogans minoribus, inter pares difficilis,: omnem adrogantem humilia,: abominatio Domino est omnis adrogans,: beatos dicimus adrogantes,.—Adv.: arrŏgan-ter (adr-), with assumption, arrogantly, haughtily, proudly, insolently: aliquid dicere,; ; : scribere,: aliquid praejudicare,: petere,: adsentire,: facere,: adversarios sustinere, D. Brutus ap. : ingredi, * : consulere in deditos,.—Comp.: multo adrogantius factum,: insolentius et adrogantius uti gloriā artis,: adrogantius et elatius praefari,.—Sup., ; .

la:noun:arrogantia.html:
arrŏgantia (adr-), ae, f.
arrogans
.
An assuming, presumption, arrogance, conceitedness (syn.: superbia, insolentia, fastus): cum omnis adrogantia odiosa est, tum illa ingenii atque eloquentiae multo molestissima,: P. Crassus sine adrogantiā gravis esse videbatur et sine segnitiā verecundus,: illud γνῶθι σεαυτόν noli putare ad adrogantiam minuendam solum esse dictum, et saep.: Pallas tristi adrogantiā taedium sui moverat,: adrogantiā depravatus,: adrogantia tua decepit te,.—
The proud, lordly bearing arising from a consciousness of real or supposed superiority, pride, haughtiness (cf. arrogans): hujus adrogantiam pertinacia aequabat,: avaritia et adrogantia praecipua validiorum vitia,: tristitiam et adrogantiam et avaritiam exuerat: nec illi, quod est rarissimum, aut facilitas auctoritatem aut severitas amorem deminuit,: cum magnitudinem et gravitatem summae fortunae retineret, invidiam et adrogantiam effugerat,; : adrogantia ejus,; .—*
A pertinacity in one's demands, obstinacy: cessurosque se potius adrogantiae Antipatri quam etc.,

la:verb:arrideo.html:
ar-rīdĕo (adr-, Lachm., B. and K., Halm, K. and H.; arr-, Fleck., Merk., Weissenb.), rīsi, rīsum, 2, v. n.,
to laugh at or with, to smile at or upon, especially approvingly.
Lit., constr. absol. or with dat., more rarely with acc.; also pass.—
Absol.: si non arriderent, dentis ut restringerent,: oportet lenam probam arridere Quisquis veniat, blandeque alloqui,: cum quidam familiaris (Dionysii) jocans dixisset: huic (juveni) quidem certe vitam tuam committis, adrisissetque adulescens, utrumque jussit interfici,: Hic cum adrisisset ipse Crassus,; ; : Cum risi, arrides,: Cum adrisissent, discessimus,; so * .—
With dat.: Tum mi aedes quoque arridebant,: si dentibus adrident,: nulli laedere os, arridere omnibus,; : vix notis familiariter arridere,.—
With acc.: video quid adriseris,: Cn. Flavius id adrisit, laughed at this, Piso ap. : vos nunc alloquitur, vos nunc adridet ocellis, Val. .—
Pass.: si adriderentur, esset id ipsum Atticorum, (B. and K., riderentur). —
Trop.
Subject., to be favorable, kindly disposed to one: cum tempestas adridet,: et quandoque mihi Fortunae adriserit hora,.—
Object. (i. e. in reference to the effect produced), to be pleasing to, to please: inhibere illud tuum, quod valde mihi adriserat, vehementer displicet,: quibus haec adridere velim,.
